strengths: The paper identifies an underexplored but practically important issue in few-shot 3D point-cloud segmentation: prototype construction and the sensitivity of FPS-based prototypes to initialization.

WARM is simple and conceptually coherent, combining whitening, cross-attention, and coloring to make learnable prototype generation compatible with support features while restoring instance statistics.

The empirical gains are substantial and broadly consistent across S3DIS and ScanNet, both folds, and all reported 1/2-way and 1/5-shot settings. The overall improvements over the strongest listed baseline are particularly convincing on S3DIS.

The use of the same frozen Stratified Transformer backbone and leakage-controlled preprocessing improves the relevance of the comparisons. The simple FPS plus nearest-prototype baseline is also informative and exposes the importance of prototype quality.
The paper is clear and visually polished, and includes component, attention, optimization, and token-count analyses alongside qualitative results.
weaknesses: The central ablation does not isolate the contribution of coloring: it compares naive attention, normalization or whitening alone, and normalization/whitening plus coloring, but omits cross-attention plus coloring without alignment. Since normalization and whitening alone catastrophically reduce mIoU from 47.29 to 14.18 and 10.83, while adding coloring raises it to 57.59 and 60.16, the reported evidence cannot establish whether whitening is the main cause of the gain or whether coloring accounts for most of it.

The claimed semantic mechanism is only indirectly supported. Higher attention entropy demonstrates more diffuse attention, not that attended points are semantically related; the diversity statistic and a small qualitative selection likewise do not establish semantic correspondence. Region- or class-level attention purity and stronger controlled comparisons would better support this claim.

The mathematical and implementation specification of ZCA whitening is incomplete. No regularizer or eigenvalue handling is given for singular or ill-conditioned class covariance matrices, and the feature dimension is unspecified. Moreover, with the covariance normalization in Eq. 8, Eq. 9 yields Z^T Z=(L_C-1)I rather than the stated I. These issues materially affect reproducibility and numerical stability.

The FPS-instability experiment uses episode-wise ranking over 1,000 initializations, so its maximum and minimum effectively aggregate oracle-best and oracle-worst choices separately for every episode rather than representing ordinary end-to-end runs with different random seeds. No confidence intervals or repeated-training results are reported, despite robustness and optimization stability being central motivations.

The comparison set is narrow for an ECCV 2026 submission and relies partly on results reproduced by a prior paper. There are no matched reimplementations, parameter/runtime/memory comparisons, or statistical significance tests. Thus the current-state-of-the-art and efficiency claims are not fully established.

Ablations are restricted to S3DIS S0 in the 1-way 1-shot setting, while several design choices remain untested, including the simplification loss, separate foreground/background token banks, whitening regularization, and averaging independently generated prototypes in multi-shot inference. Figure 6 also appears to use test performance for token-count selection, raising a possible test-set tuning concern.

strengths: The paper identifies an underexplored component of few-shot point-cloud segmentation—prototype construction—and proposes a conceptually simple whitening–attention–coloring module.

The reported results are promising: WARM improves the strong FPS plus nearest-prototype baseline across all aggregate settings and yields overall mIoU gains from 51.03 to 55.66 on S3DIS and from 39.01 to 41.21 on ScanNet.

Evaluation covers two established datasets, two folds, 1/2-way and 1/5-shot protocols, a component ablation, prototype-count sensitivity, qualitative predictions, and attention/optimization diagnostics.
The method is generally presented clearly, and using a frozen backbone helps focus the study on prototype generation.
weaknesses: The central FPS-instability evidence in Table 1 is misleading. The authors rank 1,000 initializations independently inside every episode and aggregate corresponding ranks, producing an oracle-best versus oracle-worst spread rather than the variance of complete evaluation runs. Since normal evaluation averages many episodes, this construction can greatly exaggerate practical instability. Results across ordinary independent seeds are needed.

The state-of-the-art comparison is incomplete. In particular, the recent localization-and-expansion method discussed and cited as [20] is absent from Tables 3–4 without explanation. Consequently, the SOTA claim is not established. WARM also underperforms COSeg in ScanNet 1-way 1-shot despite the broad superiority language.

No repeated-training results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This is especially problematic for episodic evaluation and for small differences such as 30.15 versus 30.13 mIoU in ScanNet 2-way 1-shot.

The ablations do not cleanly establish the claimed mechanism. Whitening or normalization without restoration catastrophically reduces accuracy, while restoration produces most of the recovery, but there is no restoration-only control or comparison against simpler learned/deterministic prototype construction. Thus it remains unclear whether semantic cross-attention, rather than distribution recalibration, causes the gains.

High attention entropy only demonstrates diffuse attention, not aggregation of semantically related points; lower inter-token diversity could alternatively indicate prototype redundancy or collapse. The paper lacks a direct semantic-coherence measure, and this analysis is restricted to foreground examples from one S3DIS split.

Important implementation details are missing, including covariance regularization, treatment of small or rank-deficient class samples, eigendecomposition/backpropagation details, attention architecture and token initialization, and the precise extension from the foreground/background formulation to multi-way episodes. Equation (9) is undefined for singular covariance matrices, and the stated identity Z^T Z=I also omits the covariance normalization factor.

Per-episode ZCA whitening and coloring can require expensive and potentially unstable matrix decompositions, yet the paper reports no runtime, memory, numerical-stability, or computational-cost comparison. Overall, the method and results have merit, but the incomplete comparison and insufficient evidence for the central motivation and mechanism slightly favor rejection.

strengths: This is a clear Algorithms/General contribution: WARM replaces unstable FPS-based prototype construction with a differentiable whitening–cross-attention–coloring module tailored to few-shot 3D point-cloud segmentation.

The empirical gains are broad and substantial. WARM obtains the best reported overall mIoU on S3DIS (55.66 versus 51.03 for the strongest baseline) and ScanNet (41.21 versus 39.01), with improvements across all 1/2-way and 1/5-shot settings.

The evidence is coherent and mechanism-oriented: component ablations, attention entropy/diversity, qualitative attention maps, optimization curves, and token-count sensitivity complement the principal benchmark comparisons.
The simple nearest-prototype prediction pipeline strengthens the result by showing that the gains do not depend on a sophisticated decoder.
The manuscript is well organized and visually clear, with useful implementation details concerning the frozen backbone, episode counts, optimizer, schedule, token count, and hardware.
weaknesses: The whitening operation is insufficiently specified for correctness and reproducibility. Equation (9) directly uses the inverse square root of a per-class covariance matrix without explaining numerical regularization, eigenvalue truncation, or rank-deficient cases. Small foreground subsets can make this covariance singular. Moreover, given the normalization in Equation (8), the stated identity Z^T Z = I is missing a scale factor.

The central stability claim is not fully validated. Table 1 measures FPS sensitivity, but WARM is not evaluated across repeated training seeds or matched episode resampling. Thus, the evidence establishes deterministic prototype generation conditional on fixed learned parameters, not overall run-to-run stability. Confidence intervals are also absent.

The comparison set is incomplete: the relevant localization-and-expansion method cited as [20] is discussed but omitted from Tables 3–4. It is also not completely clear that all reproduced or borrowed baselines use identical backbone pretraining, preprocessing, leakage controls, and episode sampling.

Some mechanistic conclusions exceed what the measurements establish. Higher attention entropy, lower diversity, and smaller query-key distance do not alone demonstrate semantically meaningful grouping; the distance reduction may partly follow mechanically from feature rescaling. Semantic-purity or region-consistency measurements would provide stronger evidence.

Reproducibility would benefit from pseudocode and details about differentiating through the per-episode eigendecomposition, attention heads and projection dimensions, multi-way covariance handling, numerical stabilization, and runtime/memory overhead. A focused limitations discussion should also address covariance estimation for very small foreground regions.

strengths: Evaluated as an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper identifies an underexplored and practically important source of instability in few-shot 3D point-cloud segmentation: FPS-based prototype construction.

WARM is simple and well motivated: whitening support features before cross-attention and restoring their statistics afterward provides a coherent way to make learnable tokens usable without a heavy decoder.

The empirical gains are substantial on S3DIS: WARM reaches 55.66 overall mIoU versus 51.03 for the strong FPS-plus-minimum-distance baseline and 50.19 for MM-FSS. It also improves COSeg from 46.31 to 59.26 and MM-FSS from 49.84 to 52.62 when substituted for their prototype generators.

The experimental coverage is strong, including two datasets, four few-shot settings, component and loss ablations, token-count sensitivity, numerical-regularization analysis, runtime and memory measurements, attention diagnostics, and compatibility with both uniform-sampling and foreground-oversampling frameworks.

The comparison with normalization/de-normalization is particularly useful: its 57.59 mIoU versus WARM's 60.16 isolates a meaningful benefit from decorrelation beyond ordinary per-channel standardization.

The method is computationally practical and markedly faster than sequential FPS over much of the tested range, while adding only modest memory overhead. The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is not fully established. High attention entropy only demonstrates diffuse attention, not aggregation of semantically related points; diversity actually decreases from 0.8824 to 0.6442. Figure 4 is suggestive but lacks a quantitative semantic-coherence or part-consistency measure.

The stability comparison in Table 1 is potentially misleading: stochastic FPS inference is varied while WARM is assigned zero variability because it is deterministic. Training-seed variation is not reported, nor are FPS results averaged over repeated samplings or compared with a deterministic FPS initialization. This weakens both the instability argument and confidence in single-number benchmark comparisons.

No confidence intervals or repeated-training statistics are provided despite the paper emphasizing randomness and stability. The large reported FPS ranges make uncertainty estimates especially important for fair method ranking.

There is a mathematical error in the whitening description: with S=(F−mu)^T(F−mu)/(L−1), Equation 8 gives Z^T Z=(L−1)I in the full-rank unregularized case, not I as claimed. Eigenvalue clipping further prevents exact whitening. This is correctable but should be fixed and the resulting scale discussed.

Whitening the support features does not by itself guarantee alignment with unconstrained learned tokens. The reported distance reduction is partly an immediate consequence of centering and rescaling, so the stronger claim that WARM establishes a shared semantic space needs more direct evidence.

The contribution is an effective but relatively incremental combination of established whitening, cross-attention, and coloring operations. ScanNet performance is competitive rather than state of the art, trailing multimodal MM-FSS overall by 3.32 mIoU.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract's public-code URL is blank, and details such as attention heads, projection dimensions or scaling, initialization, augmentation, and all implementation choices needed to reproduce the module are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant, underexplored issue in few-shot 3D point-cloud segmentation: prototype construction and the inference-time variability introduced by randomly initialized farthest-point sampling.

WARM is conceptually simple and computationally practical, combining ZCA whitening, cross-attention, and coloring without a heavy decoder. The runtime and memory measurements suggest reasonable overhead.

The empirical evaluation covers S3DIS and ScanNet across 1/2-way and 1/5-shot settings. WARM improves the simple FPS-plus-nearest-prototype baseline overall on both datasets, with particularly strong results on S3DIS.

The component, loss, token-count, compatibility, and numerical-regularization studies provide useful diagnostic evidence. Integrating WARM into COSeg and MM-FSS also suggests some plug-and-play value.
The manuscript is generally organized and provides equations, implementation settings, qualitative examples, and supplementary numerical-stability details.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol appears to use test episodes for method development. Section 6.2 states that ablations are conducted on test episodes of S3DIS split S0, and supplementary Table A1 uses their mIoU to motivate the selected whitening threshold. This is test-set hyperparameter selection and compromises at least the S0 results and aggregate comparisons unless the authors can establish a strictly separate validation procedure.

The central stability claim is not convincingly evaluated. Table 1 measures randomness from FPS initialization but reports no variance across training seeds, episode draws, or model initialization for WARM. Its zero variance is therefore largely a consequence of deterministic inference. A fair study should compare repeated end-to-end runs and simple deterministic FPS variants, such as a fixed or centroid-based initial point.

The evidence does not isolate whitening as the main source of improvement. In Table 5, normalization plus de-normalization already reaches 57.59 mIoU versus 60.16 for whitening plus coloring; thus whitening contributes only 2.57 points there, while restoration accounts for most of the gain over vanilla attention. Comparisons with masked averaging, statistics-conditioned tokens, deterministic sampling, and stronger normalization alternatives are needed.

The interpretation of the attention analysis is weak. Higher attention entropy demonstrates broader or more uniform attention, not semantic coherence, and WARM simultaneously lowers inter-token diversity. The reported metrics therefore do not establish the claimed semantic grouping; class- or part-aware quantitative measurements and appropriate uniform-attention controls would be more probative.

The proposed alignment mechanism is insufficiently justified technically. Only support features are whitened, while the learnable tokens are not subjected to the same transformation; making one distribution zero-mean and decorrelated does not by itself prove that it is aligned with another distribution. Moreover, with the covariance definition in Eq. (7), Eq. (8) gives Z^T Z=(L_C-1)I rather than the stated I.

The headline gains do not generalize uniformly. WARM is strong on S3DIS but trails multimodal MM-FSS overall on ScanNet (41.21 versus 44.53), and the plug-in experiments are reported only for a limited S3DIS setting rather than across datasets and episode configurations.

Originality is limited for an Algorithms/General submission: the method primarily wraps standard ZCA whitening and its inverse around conventional cross-attention. Given that the whitening-specific improvement is modest, the paper needs stronger controlled evidence or a deeper theoretical account to establish a sufficiently substantial contribution.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including token initialization, exact cross-attention architecture, projection/head configuration, whether and how the backbone is updated, augmentation and episode-sampling details, and results over independent training runs. The abstract's code-availability field is also blank in the submitted manuscript.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. The paper identifies a meaningful weakness in the standard FPS-based prototype pipeline for few-shot 3D point-cloud segmentation: predictions can vary substantially with FPS initialization. Replacing this heuristic with deterministic learned aggregation is well motivated and relevant to computer vision.

WARM is simple and technically intuitive: ZCA whitening standardizes support features before cross-attention, while coloring restores instance-specific statistics afterward. The design adds only a modest module and avoids a complex segmentation decoder.

The empirical results are strong. WARM improves the simple FPS baseline from 51.03 to 55.66 overall mIoU on S3DIS and consistently improves it across all reported splits and shot/way settings. Results on ScanNet are also consistently better than the unimodal FPS baseline, although below the multimodal MM-FSS overall.

The experimental analysis is unusually broad: component and loss ablations, normalization versus whitening, token-count sensitivity, parameter-capacity controls, attention diagnostics, runtime and memory measurements, numerical-stability studies, and integration into COSeg, MM-FSS, and VIP-Seg all support the practical value of the module.

The compatibility results are particularly compelling: replacing FPS with WARM raises COSeg by 12.95 mIoU and also improves MM-FSS and VIP-Seg. This suggests that the contribution is not merely tied to the paper's minimal prediction head.

The paper is clear and visually polished, supplies major implementation and evaluation details, evaluates 1/2-way and 1/5-shot regimes on both standard datasets and both class splits, and explicitly discusses the different uniform-sampling and foreground-oversampling protocols.
weaknesses: The central stability claim is only partially established. Table 1 measures sensitivity to FPS randomness, but WARM's identical outputs follow directly from deterministic inference. The paper does not report variation across independent training seeds, episode sampling, or backbone initialization, even though training itself remains stochastic. Confidence intervals or multi-run means would make the claimed robustness substantially more convincing.

The proposed causal interpretation is stronger than the evidence. Whitening maps support features to a standardized space, but the paper does not explain what explicitly constrains the learned prototypical tokens to have the same distribution. Likewise, high attention entropy demonstrates diffuse attention, not by itself semantically coherent aggregation; the accompanying decrease in inter-token diversity could also indicate more redundant prototypes. Direct semantic-purity, coverage, or token-redundancy measurements would better validate this explanation.

Most diagnostic and ablation experiments are restricted to S3DIS split S0 under 1-way 1-shot evaluation. Repeating the key whitening/coloring, regularization, and attention analyses on ScanNet would be valuable because the main performance margin is smaller there and the token-count behavior already differs across datasets.

Some mathematical and implementation details require correction or clarification. With the covariance definition in Eq. (7), Eq. (8) gives Z^T Z=(L-1)I rather than I as stated. The main text also defines the regularization threshold using the median eigenvalue without immediately specifying that only positive eigenvalues are considered; this matters when L≤D and the covariance is rank deficient. It is also unclear whether the pretrained backbone is frozen or fine-tuned.

The novelty is moderate: whitening/coloring and cross-attention are established tools, with the main contribution being their effective combination and task-specific analysis. The strong gains and plug-and-play evidence compensate for this, but the paper should position the method more explicitly relative to prior whitening-based attention or feature-alignment approaches.

The principal comparisons are episode means without uncertainty estimates, and the discrepancy between the FPS baseline's mean in Table 1 (49.48) and its S0 result in Table 3 (51.35) is not explained. These reporting issues do not overturn the empirical case but make effect-size calibration harder.
